KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap ## 5.1 Part A — Short Answer Questions (3 Marks Each) ### Question 1 [KTU University Exam - May 2024] **Define a "body force" and a "surface force" in fluid mechanics. Give two examples of each.** **Model Answer:** > A **body force** is a force that acts on the entire volume of a fluid element; its magnitude is proportional to the mass or volume of the fluid. The most common body force in fluid mechanics is **gravity**. > > A **surface force** is a force that acts on the surface (boundary) of a fluid element; its magnitude is proportional to the surface area on which it acts. Surface forces include **pressure force** (normal to the surface) and **viscous shear force** (tangential to the surface). > > **Examples:** > - *Body forces*: (i) Gravity, (ii) Centrifugal force > - *Surface forces*: (i) Pressure force, (ii) Viscous shear force ### Question 2 [KTU University Exam - Dec 2023] **State Bernoulli's equation. List the assumptions made in its derivation.** **Model Answer:** > **Bernoulli's Equation** states that for a steady, incompressible, inviscid flow along a streamline, the sum of the pressure head, velocity head, and elevation head is constant: > > $$\frac{P}{\rho g} + \frac{V^2}{2g} + z = \text{constant}$$ > > **Assumptions:** > 1. The flow is **steady** ($\frac{\partial \vec{V}}{\partial t} = 0$). > 2. The fluid is **incompressible** ($\rho = \text{constant}$). > 3. The fluid is **inviscid** ($\mu = 0$, no viscous effects). > 4. The equation is applied **along a streamline**. > 5. **No shaft work** (no pumps or turbines in the flow region). > 6. The fluid is **ideal** and the flow is **continuous**. --- ## 5.2 Part B — 14-Mark Questions (Module Internal Choice) ### Question A (Choice 1) [KTU University Exam - Dec 2024] #### (a) [7 Marks] Derive Euler's equation of motion in three dimensions for an inviscid fluid. **Model Solution:** Consider an infinitesimally small fluid element — a parallelepiped of dimensions $dx$, $dy$, $dz$ — moving with the fluid. Let $P$ be the pressure at the center of the element. **Step 1: Compute the Body Force** The only body force is gravity, acting in the negative $z$-direction. The body force per unit volume is: $$ \vec{f}_b = -\rho g \hat{k} $$ **Step 2: Compute the Pressure Force** The pressure on the face at $x + \frac{dx}{2}$ is $P + \frac{\partial P}{\partial x}\frac{dx}{2}$ and on the face at $x - \frac{dx}{2}$ is $P - \frac{\partial P}{\partial x}\frac{dx}{2}$. Net pressure force in the $x$-direction: $$ F_{p,x} = \left(P - \frac{\partial P}{\partial x}\frac{dx}{2}\right)dy\,dz - \left(P + \frac{\partial P}{\partial x}\frac{dx}{2}\right)dy\,dz = -\frac{\partial P}{\partial x}dx\,dy\,dz $$ Similarly, the net pressure forces in the $y$ and $z$ directions are: $$ F_{p,y} = -\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}dx\,dy\,dz, \quad F_{p,z} = -\frac{\partial P}{\partial z}dx\,dy\,dz $$ The total pressure force is therefore: $$ \vec{F}_p = -\left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial x}\hat{i} + \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\hat{j} + \frac{\partial P}{\partial z}\hat{k}\right)dx\,dy\,dz $$ **Step 3: For an Inviscid Fluid, Viscous Force = 0** **Step 4: Acceleration of the Fluid Element** Using the material derivative: $$ a_x = \frac{Du}{Dt} = \frac{\partial u}{\partial t} + u\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} + v\frac{\partial u}{\partial y} + w\frac{\partial u}{\partial z} $$ **Step 5: Apply Newton's Second Law** Total force = mass × acceleration. Dividing by volume $dx\,dy\,dz$: $$ -\frac{\partial P}{\partial x} = \rho\frac{Du}{Dt} $$ $$ -\frac{\partial P}{\partial y} = \rho\frac{Dv}{Dt} $$ $$ -\frac{\partial P}{\partial z} - \rho g = \rho\frac{Dw}{Dt} $$ **Step 6: Combine in Vector Form** $$ \boxed{-\nabla P + \rho\vec{g} = \rho\frac{D\vec{V}}{Dt}} $$ This is **Euler's equation of motion** in 3D vector form. #### (b) [7 Marks] A pipe of diameter 300 mm at section 1 carries water at a velocity of 5 m/s. At section 2, which is 4 m above section 1, the diameter is 200 mm. If the pressure at section 1 is 150 kPa, find the pressure at section 2. Assume ideal flow. **Given:** - $D_1 = 300 \, \text{mm} = 0.3 \, \text{m}$, $V_1 = 5 \, \text{m/s}$ - $D_2 = 200 \, \text{mm} = 0.2 \, \text{m}$, $z_2 - z_1 = 4 \, \text{m}$ - $P_1 = 150 \, \text{kPa} = 150{,}000 \, \text{Pa}$ - $\rho_{\text{water}} = 1000 \, \text{kg/m}^3$, $g = 9.81 \, \text{m/s}^2$ **Model Solution:** **Step 1: Use the Continuity Equation to find $V_2$** $$ A_1 V_1 = A_2 V_2 $$ $$ V_2 = V_1 \cdot \frac{A_1}{A_2} = V_1 \cdot \left(\frac{D_1}{D_2}\right)^2 = 5 \times \left(\frac{0.3}{0.2}\right)^2 = 5 \times 2.25 = 11.25 \, \text{m/s} $$ **Step 2: Apply Bernoulli's Equation** $$ \frac{P_1}{\rho g} + \frac{V_1^2}{2g} + z_1 = \frac{P_2}{\rho g} + \frac{V_2^2}{2g} + z_2 $$ Rearranging for $P_2$: $$ P_2 = P_1 + \rho g \left(\frac{V_1^2 - V_2^2}{2g}\right) - \rho g(z_2 - z_1) $$ **Step 3: Substitute Values** $$ P_2 = 150{,}000 + 1000 \times 9.81 \times \left(\frac{5^2 - 11.25^2}{2 \times 9.81}\right) - 1000 \times 9.81 \times 4 $$ $$ P_2 = 150{,}000 + \frac{1000 \times (25 - 126.5625)}{2} - 39{,}240 $$ $$ P_2 = 150{,}000 + \frac{-101{,}562.5}{2} - 39{,}240 $$ $$ P_2 = 150{,}000 - 50{,}781.25 - 39{,}240 $$ $$ \boxed{P_2 = 59{,}978.75 \, \text{Pa} \approx 59.98 \, \text{kPa}} $$ --- ### Question B (Choice 2) [KTU University Exam - May 2024] #### (a) [7 Marks] Starting from Euler's equation of motion, derive Bernoulli's equation for steady, incompressible, inviscid flow along a streamline. **Model Solution:** **Step 1: Write Euler's Equation in Component Form** $$ -\frac{\partial P}{\partial x} = \rho\left(\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} + u\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} + v\frac{\partial u}{\partial y} + w\frac{\partial u}{\partial z}\right) $$ $$ -\frac{\partial P}{\partial y} = \rho\left(\frac{\partial v}{\partial t} + u\frac{\partial v}{\partial x} + v\frac{\partial v}{\partial y} + w\frac{\partial v}{\partial z}\right) $$ $$ -\frac{\partial P}{\partial z} - \rho g = \rho\left(\frac{\partial w}{\partial t} + u\frac{\partial w}{\partial x} + v\frac{\partial w}{\partial y} + w\frac{\partial w}{\partial z}\right) $$ **Step 2: Apply Steady Flow Assumption** For steady flow, all local derivatives vanish: $\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} = \frac{\partial v}{\partial t} = \frac{\partial w}{\partial t} = 0$. **Step 3: Multiply x-equation by $dx$, y-equation by $dy$, z-equation by $dz$ and add** $$ -\frac{\partial P}{\partial x}dx - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}dy - \frac{\partial P}{\partial z}dz = \rho\left(u\,du + v\,dv + w\,dw\right) + \rho g \cdot (-dz) $$ The left side is $-dP$ (total differential of pressure). The right side is $\rho \cdot d\left(\frac{V^2}{2}\right) - \rho g\,dz$ since $u\,du + v\,dv + w\,dw = \frac{1}{2}d(u^2 + v^2 + w^2) = \frac{1}{2}d(V^2)$. **Step 4: Combine into a Single Differential Equation** $$ dP + \rho \cdot \frac{1}{2}d(V^2) + \rho g\,dz = 0 $$ **Step 5: Apply Incompressibility ($\rho$ = constant) and Integrate** Dividing by $\rho$ and integrating from point 1 to point 2: $$ \int_1^2 \frac{dP}{\rho} + \int_1^2 \frac{1}{2}d(V^2) + \int_1^2 g\,dz = 0 $$ $$ \frac{P_2 - P_1}{\rho} + \frac{V_2^2 - V_1^2}{2} + g(z_2 - z_1) = 0 $$ **Step 6: Rearrange to Obtain Bernoulli's Equation** $$ \frac{P_1}{\rho} + \frac{V_1^2}{2} + g z_1 = \frac{P_2}{\rho} + \frac{V_2^2}{2} + g z_2 $$ **Final Result:** $$ \boxed{\frac{P}{\rho} + \frac{V^2}{2} + gz = \text{constant (along a streamline)}} $$ This is **Bernoulli's equation** in energy-per-unit-mass form. #### (b) [7 Marks] Water flows through a venturi meter with inlet diameter 200 mm and throat diameter 100 mm. The differential manometer shows a mercury deflection of 200 mm. Calculate the discharge through the venturi meter, assuming the coefficient of discharge is 0.98. **Given:** - $D_1 = 200 \, \text{mm} = 0.2 \, \text{m}$ (inlet diameter) - $D_2 = 100 \, \text{mm} = 0.1 \, \text{m}$ (throat diameter) - $h = 200 \, \text{mm} = 0.2 \, \text{m}$ (manometer deflection) - $C_d = 0.98$ (coefficient of discharge) - $S_m = 13.6$ (specific gravity of mercury) **Model Solution:** **Step 1: Compute the Area Ratio** $$ \frac{A_1}{A_2} = \left(\frac{D_1}{D_2}\right)^2 = \left(\frac{0.2}{0.1}\right)^2 = 4 $$ **Step 2: Compute the Differential Head (in terms of water)** The differential manometer reads a mercury column height $h$. The equivalent water head difference is: $$ x = h \left(\frac{S_m}{S_w} - 1\right) = 0.2 \times (13.6 - 1) = 0.2 \times 12.6 = 2.52 \, \text{m of water} $$ **Step 3: Use the Venturi Discharge Formula** The theoretical discharge through a venturi meter is: $$ Q_{th} = \frac{A_1 A_2 \sqrt{2g x}}{\sqrt{A_1^2 - A_2^2}} $$ This is derived from combining the **continuity equation** and **Bernoulli's equation**. Simplification using $A_1 = 4A_2$: $$ A_1^2 - A_2^2 = 16A_2^2 - A_2^2 = 15A_2^2 $$ $$ A_1 A_2 = 4A_2^2 $$ $$ Q_{th} = \frac{4A_2^2 \sqrt{2 \times 9.81 \times 2.52}}{\sqrt{15A_2^2}} = \frac{4A_2^2 \sqrt{49.44}}{A_2 \sqrt{15}} = \frac{4 A_2 \times 7.0314}{3.873} $$ **Step 4: Compute the Throat Area** $$ A_2 = \frac{\pi}{4}D_2^2 = \frac{\pi}{4}(0.1)^2 = 0.007854 \, \text{m}^2 $$ **Step 5: Compute the Theoretical Discharge** $$ Q_{th} = \frac{4 \times 0.007854 \times 7.0314}{3.873} = \frac{0.2209}{3.873} = 0.05704 \, \text{m}^3/\text{s} $$ **Step 6: Apply the Coefficient of Discharge** $$ Q_{actual} = C_d \times Q_{th} = 0.98 \times 0.05704 $$ $$ \boxed{Q_{actual} = 0.0559 \, \text{m}^3/\text{s} \approx 55.9 \, \text{L/s}} $$ --- ## 5.3 KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning / Pitfall Callout > [!WARNING] > **Common Mark-Loss Pitfalls in KTU Valuation:** > > 1. **Forgetting assumptions of Bernoulli's equation**: KTU examiners typically award 1 mark for explicitly listing all assumptions (steady, incompressible, inviscid, along streamline, no shaft work). Students often skip this and lose easy marks. > > 2. **Sign convention error in pressure force derivation**: The pressure force in the $x$-direction is $-\frac{\partial P}{\partial x} dV$. Students often miss the negative sign and write $+\frac{\partial P}{\partial x} dV$, which is a common mistake. > > 3. **Units inconsistency**: Ensure SI units throughout. Pressure should be in **Pa** (N/m²), velocity in **m/s**, and elevation in **m**. A common error is using kPa without converting to Pa. > > 4. **Bernoulli's equation is along a streamline, NOT between any two points in the flow field** (unless the flow is irrotational). This subtle distinction is tested in Part A. > > 5. **Material derivative confusion**: Students often write $\frac{\partial \vec{V}}{\partial t}$ as the acceleration. Remember, the acceleration is the **material derivative** $\frac{D\vec{V}}{Dt}$, which includes convective terms. > > 6. **For venturi meter problems, the manometer reading $h$ is in mm of mercury**, and the equivalent water head must be calculated using $x = h(S_m/S_w - 1)$. Direct substitution of $h$ in Bernoulli's equation is a frequent error. > > 7. **Show the integration step clearly** in Bernoulli's derivation. The integral $\int V\,dV = \frac{V^2}{2}$ is a common place where students skip steps and lose marks. --- ## 5.4 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember (Rapid Revision Checklist) > **Quick-Recall Summary (Save this for last-minute revision):** - **Forces in fluid motion** are classified into **body forces** (gravity, centrifugal) and **surface forces** (pressure, viscous). - **Body forces** are proportional to **volume/mass**; **surface forces** are proportional to **area**. - **Pressure force** is always **normal** and **inward (compressive)**; **viscous force** is **tangential** and given by $\tau = \mu \frac{du}{dy}$ for Newtonian fluids. - **Newton's second law** for a fluid element: $\sum \vec{F} = m\vec{a} = \rho V \vec{a}$. - The **true acceleration** of a fluid particle is the **material derivative**: $\frac{D\vec{V}}{Dt} = \frac{\partial \vec{V}}{\partial t} + (\vec{V}\cdot\nabla)\vec{V}$. - **Euler's equation** (inviscid): $-\nabla P + \rho \vec{g} = \rho \frac{D\vec{V}}{Dt}$. - **Bernoulli's equation** (steady, incompressible, inviscid, along streamline): $\frac{P}{\rho g} + \frac{V^2}{2g} + z = \text{constant}$. - Each term in Bernoulli's equation represents a **head** (in m of fluid): **pressure head, velocity head, elevation head**. - The **total head is constant** along a streamline for ideal flow. - Bernoulli's equation is **valid only along a streamline** (unless flow is irrotational, in which case it holds throughout). - The **Venturi effect** (high velocity → low pressure) is a direct consequence of Bernoulli's equation. - For a **real (viscous) fluid**, the **Navier–Stokes equation** is used; Bernoulli's equation is an approximation that neglects friction losses. - **Continuity equation** is often used together with Bernoulli's to solve pipe-flow problems: $A_1 V_1 = A_2 V_2$. - In **venturi meter** problems, remember: $x = h(S_m/S_w - 1)$ and $Q = C_d \cdot Q_{th}$. - **Units to remember**: $\rho$ in kg/m³, $P$ in Pa (N/m²), $V$ in m/s, $g = 9.81$ m/s², $\mu$ in N·s/m².

topics.title: Derivation of Bernoulli's Equation from Euler's Equation of Motion with Assumptions
topics.content:
> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME**
> - **Course:** PCCET302 - FLUID MECHANICS
> - **Module:** Module 2
> - **Topic:** Derivation of Bernoulli's Equation from Euler's Equation of Motion with Assumptions

<!-- SECTION_1_START -->
## 1. Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

### 1.1 Formal Academic Definition (KTU 2024 Syllabus Terminology)

**Bernoulli's Equation** is the fundamental energy conservation equation for an ideal fluid in steady, incompressible, frictionless flow along a streamline. It is mathematically derived by integrating **Euler's Equation of Motion** (which is itself Newton's second law applied to an inviscid fluid element) along a streamline.

In its standard form, Bernoulli's equation states that the sum of the pressure head, velocity head, and elevation head remains constant between any two points along a streamline:

$$\frac{p}{\gamma} + \frac{V^2}{2g} + z = \text{Constant}$$

where each term has units of length (meters) and represents a specific form of fluid energy per unit weight.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU Board Examiner Insight:** The term $\frac{p}{\gamma}$ is the **Pressure Head**, $\frac{V^2}{2g}$ is the **Velocity Head (Kinematic Energy Head)**, and $z$ is the **Elevation Head (Potential Energy Head)**. Together, they form the **Total Energy Head** of the flowing fluid.

**Euler's Equation of Motion** is the differential equation governing the motion of an inviscid (non-viscous) fluid, derived by applying Newton's second law to a fluid element moving along a streamline:

$$\frac{dp}{\rho} + g\,dz + V\,dV = 0$$

> [!NOTE]
> **Key Distinction:** Euler's equation is in *differential* form and applies to *infinitesimal* fluid elements. Bernoulli's equation is its *integrated* form, applicable between any two finite points along a streamline.

### 1.2 Conceptual Analogy — The Intuitive Picture

Imagine a small marble rolling down a smooth, frictionless, curved slide inside a sealed pipe filled with honey-like fluid. As the marble descends, it speeds up (just like a fluid element picks up velocity), and at the same time, the pressure around it changes. **Bernoulli's equation is essentially the "energy accounting ledger"** of this marble: it tells you that as the marble trades elevation for speed, the pressure must adjust to keep the total energy ledger perfectly balanced.

> [!NOTE]
> **Real-World Analogy — A Mountain Stream:**
> Picture water flowing down a steep mountain slope. At the top, water is slow and at high elevation but the pressure beneath is also high (deep). Halfway down, the water rushes faster but the elevation is lower. The sum of all three "energy forms" — pressure, motion, and elevation — remains the *same* at every point along the stream. This invariant is precisely Bernoulli's Principle.

### 1.3 Physical Constants and Standard Metrics

- **Acceleration due to gravity:** $g = 9.81 \text{ m/s}^2$ (standard) or $9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$ (KTU exam preferred)
- **Specific weight of water:** $\gamma_{water} = 9810 \text{ N/m}^3$
- **Density of water:** $\rho_{water} = 1000 \text{ kg/m}^3$

<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
## 2. Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

### 2.1 The Operational Logic: Why Derive Bernoulli from Euler?

The derivation is essentially a **two-stage mathematical journey**:

1. **Stage 1 — From Newton's Second Law to Euler's Equation:** Apply $\sum F = ma$ to a fluid element in an inviscid flow field.
2. **Stage 2 — From Euler's Equation (Differential) to Bernoulli's Equation (Integrated):** Integrate along a streamline, assuming constant density.

### 2.2 Assumptions Required for the Derivation

The transition from Euler to Bernoulli is valid **only** when the following assumptions hold simultaneously:

| # | Assumption | Mathematical Implication |
|---|------------|---------------------------|
| 1 | **Steady Flow** | $\frac{\partial V}{\partial t} = 0$ — Local acceleration is zero, so terms vanish in Euler's derivation |
| 2 | **Incompressible Flow** | $\rho = \text{constant}$ — Density can be taken out of the integration sign |
| 3 | **Inviscid (Non-viscous) Flow** | $\mu = 0$ — No shear stress; Euler's equation itself requires this |
| 4 | **Flow Along a Streamline** | Equation applies only between points on the *same* streamline |
| 5 | **No External Energy Addition/Extraction** | No pump, turbine, or shaft work between the two points |
| 6 | **Continuum Assumption** | Fluid properties are defined at every point |

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU 2024 High-Yield Point:** The most commonly tested assumption in KTU board exams is the **steady flow** assumption. If you forget it, you lose 2 marks instantly. Always write "**steady, incompressible, inviscid flow along a streamline**" as a single phrase.

### 2.3 KTU Formula Sheet / Cheat Sheet

| Formula | Expression | Meaning / Application |
|---------|------------|----------------------|
| Euler's Equation (Differential form along streamline) | $\frac{dp}{\rho} + g\,dz + V\,dV = 0$ | Starting point of the derivation |
| Euler's Equation (Vector form) | $\rho \vec{a} = -\nabla p + \rho \vec{g}$ | Foundation of all ideal-fluid dynamics |
| Integrated Euler (per unit volume) | $\frac{p}{\rho} + gz + \frac{V^2}{2} = C$ | Energy per unit volume form |
| **Bernoulli's Equation (per unit weight)** | $\frac{p}{\gamma} + \frac{V^2}{2g} + z = \text{constant}$ | **The KTU board-favorite form** |
| Bernoulli's Equation (per unit mass) | $\frac{p}{\rho} + gz + \frac{V^2}{2} = \text{constant}$ | Useful for compressible gas flow |
| Bernoulli's Equation (Energy form) | $\frac{p}{\gamma} + \frac{V^2}{2g} + z_1 = \frac{p}{\gamma} + \frac{V^2}{2g} + z_2$ | Two-point application form |
| Relation between $C$ (per unit weight) and $C'$ (per unit volume) | $C = \frac{C'}{g}$ | Conversion between the two forms |

> [!NOTE]
> **Table Notation Note:** Vertical bars `$\vert$` are used here for absolute value to avoid breaking markdown table syntax.

### 2.4 Real-World Engineering Utility

- **Venturi Meter & Orifice Meter:** Flow rate measurement in pipelines
- **Pitot Tube:** Aircraft airspeed measurement
- **Carburetor & Atomizers:** Mixing fuel with air using pressure drop
- **Hydroelectric Power Plants:** Energy conversion calculations
- **Aerofoil Lift Generation:** The core principle behind aircraft wings
- **Siphons and Tap-flow Systems:** Domestic and industrial fluid transport

<!-- SECTION_2_END -->

<!-- SECTION_3_START -->
## 3. Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

### 3.1 Derivation of Euler's Equation of Motion (Foundation)

Consider a small fluid element of cross-sectional area $dA$ and length $ds$, moving along a streamline inclined at angle $\theta$ to the horizontal. Let $z$ be the elevation of the center of the element above a chosen datum.

**Step 1 — Identify the forces acting on the element along the streamline direction:**

- **Pressure force on the upstream face (in direction of flow):** $p\,dA$
- **Pressure force on the downstream face (opposite to flow):** $(p + dp)\,dA$
- **Component of weight along the streamline (opposite to flow):** $-W\sin\theta = -\rho g\,dA\,ds\,\sin\theta$

Since $dz = ds\sin\theta$ (the vertical rise along the streamline), we can write:
$$-W\sin\theta = -\rho g\,dA\,dz$$

**Step 2 — Apply Newton's Second Law ($F = ma$) along the streamline:**

$$p\,dA - (p + dp)\,dA - \rho g\,dA\,dz = (\rho\,dA\,ds)\,\frac{dV}{dt}$$

Simplifying:

$$-dp\,dA - \rho g\,dA\,dz = \rho\,dA\,ds\,\frac{dV}{dt}$$

Dividing throughout by $dA$:

$$-dp - \rho g\,dz = \rho\,ds\,\frac{dV}{dt}$$

**Step 3 — Convert local to convective acceleration:**

Since the element moves along the streamline with velocity $V$:

$$V = \frac{ds}{dt} \quad \Rightarrow \quad \frac{dV}{dt} = V\,\frac{dV}{ds}$$

Substituting:

$$-dp - \rho g\,dz = \rho\,ds\,V\,\frac{dV}{ds} = \rho V\,dV$$

Rearranging to obtain the **Euler's Equation of Motion along a streamline**:

$$\boxed{\frac{dp}{\rho} + g\,dz + V\,dV = 0}$$

### 3.2 Derivation of Bernoulli's Equation from Euler's Equation

**Step 1 — Take Euler's equation as the starting point:**

$$\frac{dp}{\rho} + g\,dz + V\,dV = 0$$

**Step 2 — Apply the incompressibility assumption ($\rho = \text{constant}$):**

Since $\rho$ is constant, it can be moved outside the differential sign:

$$\frac{1}{\rho}dp + g\,dz + V\,dV = 0$$

> [!NOTE]
> **Critical Transition:** This is the most important step in the entire derivation. The validity of the integration in Step 3 depends on $\rho$ being a constant. Without this assumption, the equation would lead to compressible flow relations, not Bernoulli's equation.

**Step 3 — Integrate the equation between two points, Point 1 and Point 2, along the same streamline:**

$$\int_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{\rho}\,dp + \int_{1}^{2}g\,dz + \int_{1}^{2}V\,dV = 0$$

**Step 4 — Evaluate each integral separately (since the limits are constants):**

$$\frac{1}{\rho}\bigl[p\bigr]_{1}^{2} + g\bigl[z\bigr]_{1}^{2} + \frac{1}{2}\bigl[V^2\bigr]_{1}^{2} = 0$$

$$\frac{p_2 - p_1}{\rho} + g(z_2 - z_1) + \frac{V_2^2 - V_1^2}{2} = 0$$

**Step 5 — Rearrange to bring all terms to one side:**

$$\frac{p_2}{\rho} + gz_2 + \frac{V_2^2}{2} = \frac{p_1}{\rho} + gz_1 + \frac{V_1^2}{2}$$

**Step 6 — Generalize: each point on the streamline has the same value of the expression:**

$$\frac{p}{\rho} + gz + \frac{V^2}{2} = \text{Constant} \quad \text{(per unit mass form)}$$

**Step 7 — Convert to per-unit-weight form by dividing throughout by $g$ and using $\gamma = \rho g$:**

$$\frac{p}{\gamma} + z + \frac{V^2}{2g} = \text{Constant}$$

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Final KTU Board Form:**
> $$\boxed{\frac{p}{\gamma} + \frac{V^2}{2g} + z = \text{Constant (Bernoulli's Equation)}}$$
> The order of the three terms is the KTU-preferred convention: **Pressure Head + Velocity Head + Elevation Head = Total Energy Head**.

### 3.3 Analytical Matrix — Stepwise Justification

| Step | Mathematical Operation | Physical Justification |
|------|------------------------|------------------------|
| Start | $\frac{dp}{\rho} + g\,dz + V\,dV = 0$ | Newton's second law on a fluid element (Euler) |
| Substitution | Pull $\rho$ out of $dp$ term | Incompressible flow assumption |
| Integration | $\int$ across the streamline | Conservative force field (no friction losses) |
| Integration limits | Point 1 to Point 2 | Same streamline traversal |
| Final form | Sum of three heads = constant | Conservation of mechanical energy |

<!-- SECTION_3_END -->

<!-- SECTION_4_START -->
## 4. Structural Diagrams & Schematics

### 4.1 Derivation Flow Block Diagram (Mermaid)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Newtons Second Law F=ma] --> B[Apply to Fluid Element on Streamline]
    B --> C[Identify Pressure and Gravity Forces]
    C --> D[Derive Euler Equation of Motion]
    D --> E[dp by rho plus g dz plus V dV equals 0]
    E --> F{Apply Assumptions}
    F --> F1[Steady Flow]
    F --> F2[Incompressible rho constant]
    F --> F3[Inviscid mu equals 0]
    F --> F4[Flow Along Streamline]
    F1 --> G[Integrate Along Streamline]
    F2 --> G
    F3 --> G
    F4 --> G
    G --> H[Obtain Bernoulli Equation per unit mass]
    H --> I[Divide by g to get per unit weight form]
    I --> J[Final Bernoulli Equation p by gamma plus V squared by 2g plus z equals Constant]
    J --> K[Apply to Real World Problems]
    K --> K1[Venturi Meter]
    K --> K2[Pitot Tube]
    K --> K3[Orifice Meter]
    K --> K4[Aerofoil Lift]
```

### 4.2 Conceptual Block Architecture — Energy Components in Bernoulli's Equation

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph TE[Total Energy Head H]
        PH[Pressure Head p by gamma]
        VH[Velocity Head V squared by 2g]
        EH[Elevation Head z]
    end
    PH --> TE
    VH --> TE
    EH --> TE
    TE --> CONST[Equals Constant along streamline]
```

### 4.3 Assumptions Dependency Map

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    M[Bernoulli Equation Validity] --> A1[Steady Flow]
    M --> A2[Incompressible Flow]
    M --> A3[Inviscid Flow]
    M --> A4[Along a Streamline]
    M --> A5[No External Energy]
    A1 --> A1D[Allows neglect of local acceleration]
    A2 --> A2D[Allows rho outside integration]
    A3 --> A3D[Allows use of Euler equation]
    A4 --> A4D[Restricts scope of application]
    A5 --> A5D[No pump or turbine term]
```

<!-- SECTION_4_END -->

<!-- SECTION_5_START -->
## 5. KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

### 5.1 Part A Questions (3 Marks Each)

**Q1. [KTU University Exam – Dec 2023, Model]**
*State the assumptions made in the derivation of Bernoulli's equation from Euler's equation of motion.*

**Model Answer (3 Marks):**
The following assumptions are made:
1. **Steady flow:** Flow parameters do not change with time at a given location.
2. **Incompressible flow:** Fluid density $\rho$ remains constant throughout the flow field.
3. **Inviscid flow:** Fluid has zero viscosity, so no shear stress exists.
4. **Flow along a streamline:** Equation applies between two points on the same streamline.
5. **No external energy addition/removal:** No pump or turbine between the two points.

> [!NOTE]
> **Valuation Tip:** Writing all five assumptions clearly in numbered list form fetches full 3 marks. Skipping "no energy addition" loses 1 mark.

---

**Q2. [KTU University Exam – May 2024, Model]**
*Write down Euler's equation of motion along a streamline and define each term.*

**Model Answer (3 Marks):**
Euler's equation of motion along a streamline is:
$$\frac{dp}{\rho} + g\,dz + V\,dV = 0$$

where:
- $p$ = static pressure at the point
- $\rho$ = density of the fluid
- $g$ = acceleration due to gravity
- $z$ = elevation of the point above a chosen datum
- $V$ = velocity of the fluid at the point
- $d$ indicates a differential (infinitesimal) change along the streamline.

### 5.2 Part B Questions (14 Marks Each — Internal Choice)

> **ESE Module 2 — Question Paper Style (Internal Choice Between Q A and Q B)**

---

#### **Question A (14 Marks)**

**[KTU University Exam – Dec 2023, Adapted]**
*(a)* **State and explain with a neat sketch the assumptions made in the derivation of Bernoulli's equation from Euler's equation of motion.** *(7 Marks)*

*(b)* **Starting from Euler's equation of motion along a streamline, derive Bernoulli's equation for steady, incompressible, inviscid flow.** *(7 Marks)*

**Model Solution:**

**Part (a) — Assumptions (7 Marks):**

The assumptions are as follows:

1. **Steady flow:** The flow parameters (velocity, pressure, density) at any point do not change with time. Mathematically, $\frac{\partial \vec{V}}{\partial t} = 0$.

2. **Incompressible fluid:** The fluid density $\rho$ is constant throughout the flow. This is valid for liquids and for gases flowing at low speeds (Mach number less than 0.3).

3. **Inviscid (frictionless) flow:** Viscosity $\mu = 0$. Real fluids have viscosity, but the effect is neglected to use Euler's equation as the starting point.

4. **Flow along a streamline:** Bernoulli's equation is valid strictly between two points on the same streamline. It cannot be directly applied across streamlines unless the flow is irrotational.

5. **No external work or heat transfer:** Between the two points, there is no pump, turbine, compressor, or any heat source/sink.

6. **Continuum:** Fluid is treated as a continuous medium, so properties are defined at every point.

**Part (b) — Derivation (7 Marks):**

Starting from Newton's second law applied to a fluid element of area $dA$ and length $ds$ along a streamline inclined at angle $\theta$:

Net pressure force along streamline: $p\,dA - (p+dp)\,dA = -dp\,dA$

Component of weight along streamline: $-W\sin\theta = -\rho g\,dA\,dz$

Mass of element: $m = \rho\,dA\,ds$

Acceleration along streamline: $a = V\,\frac{dV}{ds}$

Applying $F = ma$:

$$-dp\,dA - \rho g\,dA\,dz = \rho\,dA\,ds\,V\,\frac{dV}{ds}$$

Dividing by $dA$:

$$-dp - \rho g\,dz = \rho V\,dV$$

Rearranging:

$$\frac{dp}{\rho} + g\,dz + V\,dV = 0 \quad \text{...(Euler's Equation)}$$

Since $\rho$ = constant, integrate along the streamline from Point 1 to Point 2:

$$\int_{1}^{2}\frac{dp}{\rho} + \int_{1}^{2}g\,dz + \int_{1}^{2}V\,dV = 0$$

$$\frac{p_2 - p_1}{\rho} + g(z_2 - z_1) + \frac{V_2^2 - V_1^2}{2} = 0$$

Rearranging:

$$\frac{p_1}{\rho} + gz_1 + \frac{V_1^2}{2} = \frac{p_2}{\rho} + gz_2 + \frac{V_2^2}{2}$$

Dividing by $g$ and using $\gamma = \rho g$:

$$\frac{p_1}{\gamma} + \frac{V_1^2}{2g} + z_1 = \frac{p_2}{\gamma} + \frac{V_2^2}{2g} + z_2 = \text{Constant}$$

This is **Bernoulli's Equation**.

---

#### **Question B (14 Marks) — Alternative Choice**

**[KTU University Exam – May 2024, Adapted]**
*(a)* **Derive Euler's equation of motion for a fluid element moving along a streamline.** *(7 Marks)*

*(b)* **Using the result obtained in part (a), derive Bernoulli's equation and list the necessary assumptions.** *(7 Marks)*

**Model Solution:**

**Part (a) — Euler's Equation Derivation (7 Marks):**

Consider a fluid element of cross-section $dA$ and length $ds$ along a streamline, with its center at elevation $z$ and inclined at angle $\theta$ to the horizontal.

Forces along the streamline:
- Upstream pressure thrust: $p\,dA$ (in direction of flow)
- Downstream pressure thrust: $(p + dp)\,dA$ (opposite to flow)
- Weight component along streamline: $W\sin\theta = \rho g\,dA\,ds\,\sin\theta$ (opposite to flow)
- Since $dz = ds\sin\theta$: weight component = $\rho g\,dA\,dz$

Net force along streamline: $F = p\,dA - (p+dp)\,dA - \rho g\,dA\,dz = -dp\,dA - \rho g\,dA\,dz$

Mass of element: $m = \rho\,dA\,ds$

Acceleration: $\frac{dV}{dt} = V\,\frac{dV}{ds}$ (for steady flow, using the chain rule)

Applying $F = ma$:

$$-dp\,dA - \rho g\,dA\,dz = \rho\,dA\,ds \cdot V\,\frac{dV}{ds}$$

Simplifying:

$$\frac{dp}{\rho} + g\,dz + V\,dV = 0 \quad \text{...(Euler's Equation of Motion)}$$

**Part (b) — Bernoulli's Equation (7 Marks):**

Starting from Euler's equation:

$$\frac{dp}{\rho} + g\,dz + V\,dV = 0$$

**Assumptions required:**
1. Steady flow
2. Incompressible fluid ($\rho$ = constant)
3. Inviscid fluid (no friction)
4. Flow along a streamline
5. No external energy addition

Since $\rho$ is constant:

$$\frac{1}{\rho}dp + g\,dz + V\,dV = 0$$

Integrating between Points 1 and 2 along the streamline:

$$\int_{p_1}^{p_2}\frac{dp}{\rho} + \int_{z_1}^{z_2}g\,dz + \int_{V_1}^{V_2}V\,dV = 0$$

$$\frac{p_2 - p_1}{\rho} + g(z_2 - z_1) + \frac{V_2^2 - V_1^2}{2} = 0$$

Rearranging:

$$\frac{p_1}{\rho} + gz_1 + \frac{V_1^2}{2} = \frac{p_2}{\rho} + gz_2 + \frac{V_2^2}{2} = \text{Constant}$$

Dividing throughout by $g$:

$$\boxed{\frac{p}{\gamma} + \frac{V^2}{2g} + z = \text{Constant (Bernoulli's Equation)}}$$

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning / Common Pitfalls:**
> 1. **Forgetting to mention "steady flow" assumption** — Costs 1 to 2 marks.
> 2. **Confusion between $dp/\rho$ and $dp/\gamma$** — KTU standard form is $p/\gamma$, not $p/\rho$, when written per unit weight.
> 3. **Skipping the $\sin\theta$ to $dz$ conversion** — Examiners want to see the geometric justification $dz = ds\sin\theta$.
> 4. **Writing $V\,dV$ as $V\,dV/dt$** — This is a common error; after substituting $a = V\,dV/ds$ and multiplying by $ds$, the result is $V\,dV$ (not divided by $t$).
> 5. **Not using proper streamline constraints** — The integration is strictly along a streamline; many students forget to mention this.
> 6. **Mixing up "per unit mass" and "per unit weight" forms** — Always state the form you are using at the start.

### 5.3 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember

- Bernoulli's equation is derived by **integrating Euler's equation** along a streamline.
- The derivation requires **five key assumptions**: steady, incompressible, inviscid flow, along a streamline, and no external energy.
- Euler's equation: $\frac{dp}{\rho} + g\,dz + V\,dV = 0$
- Bernoulli's equation (per unit weight): $\frac{p}{\gamma} + \frac{V^2}{2g} + z = \text{Constant}$
- Bernoulli's equation (per unit mass): $\frac{p}{\rho} + gz + \frac{V^2}{2} = \text{Constant}$
- The term $\frac{p}{\gamma}$ is the **pressure head**, $\frac{V^2}{2g}$ is the **velocity head**, and $z$ is the **elevation head**.
- The constant $C$ in the per-unit-weight form differs from $C'$ in the per-unit-mass form by a factor of $g$.
- Bernoulli's equation is a **statement of conservation of mechanical energy** for an ideal fluid.
- The equation is **valid only between two points on the same streamline** (unless flow is irrotational).
- The geometric conversion $dz = ds\sin\theta$ is essential to connect weight component to differential elevation.
- The acceleration transformation $a = V\,\frac{dV}{ds}$ comes from the chain rule applied to steady flow.
- **KTU Board Favorite Question Pattern:** "Derive Bernoulli's equation from Euler's equation, stating assumptions" (14 marks).
- The 14-mark questions are usually split as **7 marks for assumptions and 7 marks for derivation**.

<!-- SECTION_5_END -->

topics.content:
> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME**
> - **Course:** PCCET302 - FLUID MECHANICS
> - **Module:** Module 2
> - **Topic:** Momentum Equations and Forces on Pipe Bends**

<!-- SECTION_1_START -->
## 1. Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

### 1.1 Linear Momentum Equation — The Formal Definition

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Linear Momentum Equation (KTU 2024 Syllabus Definition):**
> The **Linear Momentum Equation** is the direct application of **Newton's Second Law of Motion** to a *finite control volume* of fluid. It states that the **net rate of change of linear momentum** of a fluid flowing steadily through a control volume equals the **sum of all external forces** acting on that control volume.

Mathematically, the differential form (per unit volume) is:

$$\sum \vec{F} = \frac{d}{dt}(m\vec{V}) = \dot{m}(\vec{V}_{out} - \vec{V}_{in})$$

For steady, incompressible flow through a control volume with multiple inlets and outlets, the integral form is:

$$\sum \vec{F} = \sum_{out} \dot{m}\,\vec{V} - \sum_{in} \dot{m}\,\vec{V}$$

where **ṁ = ρ Q** is the mass flow rate, **Q** is the volumetric discharge, and **ρ** is the fluid density.

---

### 1.2 Forces on Pipe Bends — What Does This Mean?

> [!NOTE]
> **Force on a Pipe Bend:**
> When a fluid flowing through a pipe changes direction (e.g., at a bend, elbow, or reducer), its **momentum vector changes direction**. This change in momentum must be produced by a **net external force** exerted on the fluid by the pipe walls. By **Newton's Third Law**, the fluid exerts an equal and opposite **reaction force on the pipe bend**, which the pipe support/flange must resist.

This force is critical in the design of:
- Pipe support anchorage
- Thrust blocks in water supply mains
- Hydraulic turbine draft tubes
- Bends in penstocks, refinery piping, and fire-fighting systems

---

### 1.3 Intuitive Real-World Analogy

> [!TIP]
> **Think of a Fire Hose 🎯**
> When firefighters direct a high-velocity jet from a hose, they must brace themselves firmly against the **recoil force** the water exerts on the hose. This recoil exists because the water's momentum changes from "stationary inside the hose" to "high-velocity jet leaving the nozzle." A pipe bend is the same scenario — the pipe is the "firefighter," the fluid jet is the "water," and the bend must be anchored to absorb the reaction force.

**Another simple example:** Hold a garden hose bent at 90° and let water flow. You will feel the hose kick sideways and try to straighten itself. The magnitude of this force depends on the **mass flow rate**, the **velocity**, and the **angle of deflection**.

---

### 1.4 Key Physical Constants / Standard Metrics

- Density of water at 4°C: **ρ_water = 1000 kg/m³**
- Density of air at STP: **ρ_air = 1.225 kg/m³**
- Acceleration due to gravity: **g = 9.81 m/s²**
- Specific weight of water: **γ_water = 9810 N/m³**
- Standard atmospheric pressure: **P_atm = 101.325 kPa**

<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
## 2. Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

### 2.1 The Physics Behind the Momentum Equation

The momentum equation is derived by applying Newton's Second Law to a control volume. The logical steps are:

1. **Identify a Control Volume (CV):** A fixed region in space through which fluid flows. The CV boundaries are the control surface (CS).
2. **Apply Newton's Second Law:** ΣF = d(mV)/dt. The right side represents the momentum flux.
3. **Use the Reynolds Transport Theorem (RTT):** Convect the body momentum of the fluid inside the CV to the flux of momentum crossing the CS.
4. **Steady Flow Assumption:** The storage of momentum inside the CV is zero (∂/∂t = 0). Only the flux across the CS contributes.
5. **Incompressible Flow Assumption:** ρ is constant, allowing ṁ = ρAV to be evaluated easily at each section.
6. **Force Decomposition:** Resolve all forces (pressure, body, viscous, reaction) into **x, y, z** components.
7. **Solve Component-wise:** Apply ΣF_x and ΣF_y independently to get scalar force magnitudes.

### 2.2 Why Is the Momentum Equation Needed?

The Bernoulli equation and energy equation deal with **energy** conservation. However, the magnitude and direction of **dynamic forces** exerted by flowing fluid on solid boundaries (pipes, blades, nozzles) cannot be obtained from energy considerations alone. The momentum equation fills this gap by providing a direct link between **forces** and **flow quantities**.

### 2.3 Real-World Engineering Utility

- **Hydraulic Engineering:** Design of anchor blocks and thrust blocks for bends in penstocks and large water mains.
- **Hydraulic Machines:** Analysis of forces on the runner blades of turbines and pumps (Euler's turbomachinery equation emerges from angular momentum).
- **Jet Propulsion:** Calculation of thrust in rockets and jet engines.
- **Marine Engineering:** Steering forces on rudders; reaction forces on ship propellers.
- **Chemical/Petrochemical Industry:** Pipe stress analysis, flange design, and support spacing in refineries.

### 2.4 KTU Formula Sheet / Cheat Sheet

> [!IMPORTANT]
> The following table is the **high-yield formula bank** for Module 2 numerical problems. Memorize these — at least one of them appears in almost every KTU ESE question from this module.

| # | Formula Name | Equation | Units | Remarks |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Linear Momentum Equation (Vector) | $\sum \vec{F} = \dot{m}(\vec{V}_{out} - \vec{V}_{in})$ | N | Steady, 1 inlet, 1 outlet |
| 2 | Mass Flow Rate | $\dot{m} = \rho Q = \rho A V$ | kg/s | ρ in kg/m³, A in m², V in m/s |
| 3 | Volumetric Discharge | $Q = A V$ | m³/s | For uniform velocity profile |
| 4 | Force in x-direction | $F_x = \dot{m}(V_{2x} - V_{1x}) + p_1 A_1 \cos\theta_1 - p_2 A_2 \cos\theta_2$ | N | $\theta_i$ measured from x-axis |
| 5 | Force in y-direction | $F_y = \dot{m}(V_{2y} - V_{1y}) + p_1 A_1 \sin\theta_1 - p_2 A_2 \sin\theta_2$ | N | Sign convention: up = +ve |
| 6 | Pressure thrust | $F_P = p A$ | N | $p$ = gauge or absolute consistently |
| 7 | Magnitude of resultant force | $F_R = \sqrt{F_x^2 + F_y^2}$ | N | Use Pythagoras on components |
| 8 | Direction of resultant | $\tan\alpha = \dfrac{\vert F_y \vert}{\vert F_x \vert}$ | degrees | α measured from x-axis |
| 9 | Force on horizontal 90° bend (gauge pressure) | $F_x = \rho Q^2 + p_1 A_1$, $F_y = \rho Q V_2 + p_2 A_2$ | N | $V_1$ assumed axial (x) |
| 10 | Force on reducing bend | $F_x = \rho Q (V_{2x} - V_{1x}) + p_1 A_1 - p_2 A_2 \cos\theta$ | N | Pressures from Bernoulli |

---

### 2.5 Sign Convention Used in KTU Solutions

- **Positive x-direction:** Outflow direction at the outlet (or horizontal right).
- **Positive y-direction:** Vertically upward.
- **Velocity components:** Use the **outflow direction as positive**. If a velocity points opposite, enter it as negative.
- **Pressure thrust** on the CV: Acts **inward (into the CV)** — that is, opposite to the outward normal of the CS at that section.
- **Reaction force on the pipe**: Always equal and opposite to the force exerted by fluid on the CV. KTU questions often ask for the **force on the pipe** (the anchor force), so a sign flip is required at the end.

<!-- SECTION_2_END -->

<!-- SECTION_3_START -->
## 3. Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

### 3.1 Derivation of the Linear Momentum Equation

We start from Newton's Second Law applied to a system of constant mass:

$$\sum \vec{F} = \frac{D(m\vec{V})}{Dt}$$

The right side is the material derivative of the system's linear momentum. Using the **Reynolds Transport Theorem (RTT)** to convert the system derivative to a control volume derivative, we get:

$$\frac{D(m\vec{V})}{Dt} = \frac{\partial}{\partial t}\int_{CV} \rho \vec{V}\, d\forall + \int_{CS} \rho \vec{V}\,(\vec{V}\cdot \hat{n})\, dA$$

The first integral is the **local (unsteady) accumulation** of momentum inside the CV, and the second integral is the **net convective flux** of momentum across the control surface.

For **steady flow**, the time derivative vanishes:

$$\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\int_{CV} \rho \vec{V}\, d\forall = 0$$

For **uniform velocity profiles** at inlet (1) and outlet (2), the surface integral reduces to:

$$\int_{CS} \rho \vec{V}\,(\vec{V}\cdot \hat{n})\, dA = \sum_{out} \rho V^2 A\, \hat{e}_t - \sum_{in} \rho V^2 A\, \hat{e}_t = \sum_{out}\dot{m}\vec{V} - \sum_{in}\dot{m}\vec{V}$$

Equating the forces to this flux:

$$\boxed{\sum \vec{F} = \sum_{out}\dot{m}\vec{V} - \sum_{in}\dot{m}\vec{V}}$$

This is the **Linear Momentum Equation** for steady, incompressible flow with uniform inlet/outlet velocities.

---

### 3.2 Derivation of the Force on a Pipe Bend

Consider a general pipe bend with:
- **Section 1 (inlet):** Area $A_1$, pressure $p_1$, velocity $V_1$, angle $\theta_1$ to the x-axis.
- **Section 2 (outlet):** Area $A_2$, pressure $p_2$, velocity $V_2$, angle $\theta_2$ to the x-axis.
- The bend is in the **horizontal plane**, so gravity does not contribute to x and y components.

**Step 1 — Define the Control Volume:** It is the **fluid inside the bend**, bounded by the inlet section (1), the outlet section (2), and the pipe walls (W).

**Step 2 — Identify All External Forces on the CV:**
1. $F_{Rx}, F_{Ry}$: Components of the reaction force exerted **by the pipe walls on the fluid**.
2. $p_1 A_1$: Pressure thrust at inlet (acts on the CV in the direction of inward normal).
3. $p_2 A_2$: Pressure thrust at outlet (acts on the CV in the direction of inward normal).

**Step 3 — Decompose the Pressures into x and y Components:**

At inlet, the inward normal points in the direction of incoming flow, so:

$$P_{1x} = p_1 A_1 \cos\theta_1, \quad P_{1y} = p_1 A_1 \sin\theta_1$$

At outlet, the inward normal points opposite to outgoing flow, so:

$$P_{2x} = -p_2 A_2 \cos\theta_2, \quad P_{2y} = -p_2 A_2 \sin\theta_2$$

**Step 4 — Apply the Momentum Equation in the x-direction:**

$$F_{Rx} + p_1 A_1 \cos\theta_1 - p_2 A_2 \cos\theta_2 = \dot{m}(V_2 \cos\theta_2 - V_1 \cos\theta_1)$$

Solving for $F_{Rx}$:

$$\boxed{F_{Rx} = \dot{m}(V_2 \cos\theta_2 - V_1 \cos\theta_1) + p_2 A_2 \cos\theta_2 - p_1 A_1 \cos\theta_1}$$

**Step 5 — Apply the Momentum Equation in the y-direction:**

$$F_{Ry} + p_1 A_1 \sin\theta_1 - p_2 A_2 \sin\theta_2 = \dot{m}(V_2 \sin\theta_2 - V_1 \sin\theta_1)$$

Solving for $F_{Ry}$:

$$\boxed{F_{Ry} = \dot{m}(V_2 \sin\theta_2 - V_1 \sin\theta_1) + p_2 A_2 \sin\theta_2 - p_1 A_1 \sin\theta_1}$$

**Step 6 — Force Exerted by Fluid on the Pipe (Anchor Force):**

By Newton's Third Law, the force the fluid exerts on the pipe is **equal and opposite** to the reaction force from the pipe on the fluid:

$$\vec{F}_{pipe} = -\vec{F}_{R} \quad \Rightarrow \quad F_{anchor,\,x} = -F_{Rx}, \quad F_{anchor,\,y} = -F_{Ry}$$

**Step 7 — Magnitude and Direction of Anchor Force:**

$$F_{anchor} = \sqrt{F_{anchor,\,x}^2 + F_{anchor,\,y}^2}$$

$$\alpha = \tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{\vert F_{anchor,\,y} \vert}{\vert F_{anchor,\,x} \vert}\right)$$

---

### 3.3 Special Case: Horizontal 90° Bend (Reducer Type)

This is the **most asked** configuration in KTU exams. Let:
- Inlet diameter = $D_1$, flow enters along +x axis ($\theta_1 = 0°$).
- Outlet diameter = $D_2$, flow exits along +y axis ($\theta_2 = 90°$).

Then $\cos\theta_1 = 1$, $\sin\theta_1 = 0$, $\cos\theta_2 = 0$, $\sin\theta_2 = 1$.

Substituting into the general formulas:

$$F_{Rx} = \dot{m}(0 - V_1) + 0 - p_1 A_1 = -\rho Q V_1 - p_1 A_1$$

$$F_{Ry} = \dot{m}(V_2 - 0) + p_2 A_2 - 0 = \rho Q V_2 + p_2 A_2$$

The anchor forces (force on the bend) are:

$$F_{anchor,\,x} = \rho Q V_1 + p_1 A_1 \quad (\text{acts in +x direction, tending to push inlet flange in flow direction})$$

$$F_{anchor,\,y} = -(\rho Q V_2 + p_2 A_2) \quad (\text{acts in -y direction, opposing the outlet jet thrust})$$

---

### 3.4 Worked-Out Example Problem (KTU-Style)

> **Problem:** Water ($\rho$ = 1000 kg/m³) flows steadily through a horizontal reducing bend. The inlet diameter is **300 mm** with a gauge pressure of **150 kPa**, and the outlet diameter is **150 mm** with a gauge pressure of **80 kPa**. The inlet velocity is **2 m/s** and the bend turns the flow through **60°**. Calculate the magnitude and direction of the force exerted by the fluid on the bend.

**Given Data:**
- $D_1 = 0.300$ m → $A_1 = \dfrac{\pi}{4}(0.300)^2 = 0.0707$ m²
- $D_2 = 0.150$ m → $A_2 = \dfrac{\pi}{4}(0.150)^2 = 0.01767$ m²
- $p_1 = 150{,}000$ Pa (gauge), $p_2 = 80{,}000$ Pa (gauge)
- $V_1 = 2$ m/s, deflection angle $\theta = 60°$
- $\rho = 1000$ kg/m³

**Step 1 — Find the Outlet Velocity (Continuity):**
$$Q = A_1 V_1 = 0.0707 \times 2 = 0.1414 \text{ m}^3/\text{s}$$

$$V_2 = \frac{Q}{A_2} = \frac{0.1414}{0.01767} = 8.0 \text{ m/s}$$

**Step 2 — Mass Flow Rate:**
$$\dot{m} = \rho Q = 1000 \times 0.1414 = 141.4 \text{ kg/s}$$

**Step 3 — Resolve Velocities (assume inlet along +x, outlet at 60° to +x):**
$$V_{1x} = 2 \cos 0° = 2 \text{ m/s}, \quad V_{1y} = 0$$
$$V_{2x} = 8 \cos 60° = 4 \text{ m/s}, \quad V_{2y} = 8 \sin 60° = 6.928 \text{ m/s}$$

**Step 4 — Resolve Pressure Thrusts:**
$$P_{1x} = p_1 A_1 \cos 0° = 150{,}000 \times 0.0707 = 10{,}605 \text{ N}$$
$$P_{1y} = 0$$
$$P_{2x} = -p_2 A_2 \cos 60° = -80{,}000 \times 0.01767 \times 0.5 = -706.8 \text{ N}$$
$$P_{2y} = -p_2 A_2 \sin 60° = -80{,}000 \times 0.01767 \times 0.866 = -1224 \text{ N}$$

**Step 5 — Apply Momentum Equation in x-direction:**
$$F_{Rx} + P_{1x} + P_{2x} = \dot{m}(V_{2x} - V_{1x})$$
$$F_{Rx} + 10{,}605 - 706.8 = 141.4 \times (4 - 2)$$
$$F_{Rx} + 9898.2 = 282.8$$
$$F_{Rx} = 282.8 - 9898.2 = -9615.4 \text{ N}$$

**Step 6 — Apply Momentum Equation in y-direction:**
$$F_{Ry} + P_{1y} + P_{2y} = \dot{m}(V_{2y} - V_{1y})$$
$$F_{Ry} + 0 - 1224 = 141.4 \times (6.928 - 0)$$
$$F_{Ry} - 1224 = 979.6$$
$$F_{Ry} = 979.6 + 1224 = 2203.6 \text{ N}$$

**Step 7 — Force on the Bend (Newton's Third Law — sign flip):**
$$F_{bend,\,x} = -F_{Rx} = 9615.4 \text{ N (in +x direction)}$$
$$F_{bend,\,y} = -F_{Ry} = -2203.6 \text{ N (in -y direction)}$$

**Step 8 — Magnitude of the Force:**
$$F_{bend} = \sqrt{(9615.4)^2 + (2203.6)^2} = \sqrt{92.46 \times 10^6 + 4.86 \times 10^6} = \sqrt{97.32 \times 10^6}$$
$$F_{bend} = 9865 \text{ N} \approx 9.87 \text{ kN}$$

**Step 9 — Direction of the Force:**
$$\alpha = \tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{2203.6}{9615.4}\right) = \tan^{-1}(0.2292) = 12.91°$$

> **Final Answer:** The fluid exerts a force of approximately **9.87 kN** on the bend, directed at an angle of **12.91°** below the +x axis (i.e., 360° − 12.91° = 347.09° measured counterclockwise from +x).

---

### 3.5 Validation Check via Dimensional Analysis

$$\dot{m} \cdot V = (\text{kg/s}) \times (\text{m/s}) = \text{kg·m/s}^2 = \text{N} \quad \checkmark$$

$$p \cdot A = (\text{N/m}^2) \times (\text{m}^2) = \text{N} \quad \checkmark$$

All terms in the momentum equation have units of **Newtons (N)**, confirming dimensional consistency.

<!-- SECTION_3_END -->

<!-- SECTION_4_START -->
## 4. Structural Diagrams & Schematics

### 4.1 Control Volume for a Pipe Bend — Free Body Schematic

The following block diagram shows the **control volume (CV)** chosen for analyzing a pipe bend, identifying the inlet (1), outlet (2), and the wall reaction force components acting on the fluid.

```mermaid
    B -.->|FRy acts on fluid| E["Pipe Wall Reaction Y"]
```

### 4.2 Vector Resolution at a 90° Horizontal Bend

The diagram below maps the velocity and pressure vectors at inlet (1) and outlet (2) of a horizontal 90° bend. The convention used: **outward normal** of CS points away from CV; pressure thrust is taken in the **inward normal** direction (opposite to outward normal).

### 4.3 Algorithmic Flow — Solving a Force-on-Bend Problem

This block diagram shows the **decision flow** a student must follow when solving a KTU numerical on pipe bend forces. It maps the dependencies between given data, intermediate quantities, and the final answer.

```mermaid

    B1 --> C1["Compute areas A1 and A2"]

    D1 --> E1["Compute mass flow rate m_dot = rho times Q"]
```

## 5. KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

### 5.1 Part A — Short Answer Questions (3 Marks Each)

> **[KTU University Exam – May 2024]**
> **Q1. State and explain Newton's Second Law of Motion as applied to a control volume of fluid. (3 Marks)**
>
> **Model Answer:**
> Newton's Second Law states that the net external force acting on a body equals the rate of change of its linear momentum. For a fluid control volume, this becomes the **Linear Momentum Equation**:
> $$\sum \vec{F} = \frac{d}{dt}\int_{CV} \rho \vec{V}\, d\forall + \int_{CS} \rho \vec{V}\,(\vec{V}\cdot\hat{n})\,dA$$
> For steady flow, the time derivative vanishes, and the equation reduces to $\sum \vec{F} = \sum_{out}\dot{m}\vec{V} - \sum_{in}\dot{m}\vec{V}$. This equation is used to find the force exerted by flowing fluid on solid boundaries such as pipe bends, nozzles, and turbine blades.

> **[KTU University Exam – Dec 2023]**
> **Q2. Define the term "control volume" and "control surface" as used in fluid mechanics. (3 Marks)**
>
> **Model Answer:**
> A **control volume (CV)** is a fixed region in space through which fluid flows; it is bounded by an arbitrary surface called the **control surface (CS)**. The control surface may be real (pipe walls) or imaginary (inlet/outlet sections). It is always closed, and the outward normal $\hat{n}$ is used to define the direction of flux across it. The CV approach allows application of conservation laws (mass, momentum, energy) to fluid flow problems in engineering systems such as turbines, pumps, and pipe networks.

---

### 5.2 Part B — Long Answer Questions (14 Marks Each — Internal Choice)

> **Note:** As per KTU 2024 ESE regulations, each Part B question carries **14 marks** with internal choice. The model answer below shows the **complete worked solution** expected at the examination.

---

#### ✅ Question A (14 Marks)

> **[KTU University Exam – Dec 2023, Modified]**
> A horizontal pipe of **300 mm diameter** carrying water ($\rho$ = 1000 kg/m³) at a velocity of **3 m/s** has a **90° bend**. The pressure at the inlet is **200 kPa (gauge)** and at the outlet is **150 kPa (gauge)**.
>
> **(a)** Derive the linear momentum equation for a control volume. (7 Marks)
> **(b)** Determine the magnitude and direction of the force exerted by the fluid on the bend. (7 Marks)

**Given:**
- $D = 0.300$ m → $A = \dfrac{\pi}{4}(0.300)^2 = 0.0707$ m²
- $V_1 = 3$ m/s, $p_1 = 200{,}000$ Pa (gauge)
- $V_2 = 3$ m/s (same diameter, so $V_2 = V_1$)
- $p_2 = 150{,}000$ Pa (gauge), deflection = 90°
- $\rho = 1000$ kg/m³

**Part (a) — Derivation of Linear Momentum Equation (7 Marks):**

Newton's Second Law for a system of constant mass is:

$$\sum \vec{F} = \frac{D(m\vec{V})}{Dt}$$

Using the **Reynolds Transport Theorem (RTT)** to switch from system to control volume:

$$\frac{D(m\vec{V})}{Dt} = \frac{\partial}{\partial t}\int_{CV} \rho \vec{V}\,d\forall + \int_{CS} \rho \vec{V}\,(\vec{V}\cdot\hat{n})\,dA$$

For **steady, incompressible** flow with uniform velocity at inlet and outlet:

$$\sum \vec{F} = \dot{m}\,\vec{V}_{out} - \dot{m}\,\vec{V}_{in}$$

Resolving into x and y components:

$$F_x = \dot{m}(V_{2x} - V_{1x}) + p_1 A_1 \cos\theta_1 - p_2 A_2 \cos\theta_2$$

$$F_y = \dot{m}(V_{2y} - V_{1y}) + p_1 A_1 \sin\theta_1 - p_2 A_2 \sin\theta_2$$

**Part (b) — Calculation of Force on the Bend (7 Marks):**

**Step 1 — Mass flow rate:**

$$\dot{m} = \rho A V_1 = 1000 \times 0.0707 \times 3 = 212.1 \text{ kg/s}$$

**Step 2 — Velocity components** (inlet along +x, outlet along +y, deflection 90°):

$$V_{1x} = 3 \text{ m/s}, \quad V_{1y} = 0$$
$$V_{2x} = 0, \quad V_{2y} = 3 \text{ m/s}$$

**Step 3 — Pressure thrusts** (inward normal directions):

At inlet ($\theta_1 = 0°$): $P_{1x} = p_1 A_1 = 200{,}000 \times 0.0707 = 14{,}140$ N, $P_{1y} = 0$
At outlet ($\theta_2 = 90°$): $P_{2x} = 0$, $P_{2y} = -p_2 A_2 = -150{,}000 \times 0.0707 = -10{,}605$ N

**Step 4 — Apply momentum in x-direction (force on fluid from pipe):**

$$F_{Rx} + P_{1x} = \dot{m}(V_{2x} - V_{1x})$$
$$F_{Rx} + 14{,}140 = 212.1 \times (0 - 3) = -636.3$$
$$F_{Rx} = -636.3 - 14{,}140 = -14{,}776.3 \text{ N}$$

**Step 5 — Apply momentum in y-direction:**

$$F_{Ry} + P_{2y} = \dot{m}(V_{2y} - V_{1y})$$
$$F_{Ry} - 10{,}605 = 212.1 \times (3 - 0) = 636.3$$
$$F_{Ry} = 636.3 + 10{,}605 = 11{,}241.3 \text{ N}$$

**Step 6 — Force on the bend (Newton's Third Law):**

$$F_{bend,\,x} = +14{,}776.3 \text{ N (in +x direction)}$$
$$F_{bend,\,y} = -11{,}241.3 \text{ N (in -y direction)}$$

**Step 7 — Magnitude:**

$$F_{bend} = \sqrt{(14{,}776.3)^2 + (11{,}241.3)^2} = \sqrt{2.183 \times 10^8 + 1.264 \times 10^8}$$
$$F_{bend} = \sqrt{3.447 \times 10^8} = 18{,}565 \text{ N} \approx 18.57 \text{ kN}$$

**Step 8 — Direction:**

$$\alpha = \tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{11{,}241.3}{14{,}776.3}\right) = \tan^{-1}(0.7607) = 37.27°$$

> **Final Answer:** The fluid exerts a force of **18.57 kN** on the bend, directed at **37.27°** below the +x axis (i.e., the anchor block must resist this force).

---

#### ✅ Question B (14 Marks) — Alternative Choice

> **[KTU University Exam – May 2024, Modified]**
> A reducing bend in a water pipeline turns the flow through **45°** in the horizontal plane. The inlet diameter is **400 mm** and the outlet diameter is **200 mm**. Water enters with a velocity of **1.5 m/s** and a pressure of **120 kPa (gauge)**. The outlet pressure is **80 kPa (gauge)**. Take $\rho$ = 1000 kg/m³.
>
> **(a)** State the assumptions made in the application of the momentum equation to a pipe bend. (5 Marks)
> **(b)** Compute the magnitude and direction of the force exerted by the water on the bend. (9 Marks)

**Part (a) — Assumptions (5 Marks):**

> [!NOTE]
> 1. **Steady flow** — flow parameters do not change with time.
> 2. **Incompressible flow** — density $\rho$ is constant (valid for liquids at moderate pressures).
> 3. **Uniform velocity profile** at inlet and outlet cross-sections (so momentum flux is $\dot{m}\vec{V}$ rather than $\int \rho V^2 dA$).
> 4. **Hydrostatic pressure distribution** at the inlet and outlet (valid for sections far from the bend where flow is nearly axial).
> 5. **Negligible frictional losses** at the wall during the short length of the bend (so we use given pressures directly; if losses are specified, Bernoulli is needed to find the missing pressure).
> 6. **Single inlet and single outlet** with no additional side branches.

**Part (b) — Calculation (9 Marks):**

**Given:**
- $D_1 = 0.400$ m → $A_1 = \dfrac{\pi}{4}(0.400)^2 = 0.1257$ m²
- $D_2 = 0.200$ m → $A_2 = \dfrac{\pi}{4}(0.200)^2 = 0.0314$ m²
- $V_1 = 1.5$ m/s, $p_1 = 120{,}000$ Pa
- $p_2 = 80{,}000$ Pa, $\theta = 45°$, $\rho = 1000$ kg/m³

**Step 1 — Outlet velocity from continuity:**

$$Q = A_1 V_1 = 0.1257 \times 1.5 = 0.1885 \text{ m}^3/\text{s}$$

$$V_2 = \frac{Q}{A_2} = \frac{0.1885}{0.0314} = 6.0 \text{ m/s}$$

**Step 2 — Mass flow rate:**

$$\dot{m} = \rho Q = 1000 \times 0.1885 = 188.5 \text{ kg/s}$$

**Step 3 — Resolve velocities (inlet along +x, outlet at 45° to +x):**

$$V_{1x} = 1.5 \text{ m/s}, \quad V_{1y} = 0$$
$$V_{2x} = 6.0 \cos 45° = 4.243 \text{ m/s}, \quad V_{2y} = 6.0 \sin 45° = 4.243 \text{ m/s}$$

**Step 4 — Resolve pressure thrusts:**

$$P_{1x} = p_1 A_1 = 120{,}000 \times 0.1257 = 15{,}080 \text{ N}, \quad P_{1y} = 0$$
$$P_{2x} = -p_2 A_2 \cos 45° = -80{,}000 \times 0.0314 \times 0.7071 = -1776.4 \text{ N}$$
$$P_{2y} = -p_2 A_2 \sin 45° = -1776.4 \text{ N}$$

**Step 5 — Apply momentum equation in x-direction:**

$$F_{Rx} + 15{,}080 - 1776.4 = 188.5 \times (4.243 - 1.5)$$
$$F_{Rx} + 13{,}303.6 = 188.5 \times 2.743 = 517.1$$
$$F_{Rx} = 517.1 - 13{,}303.6 = -12{,}786.5 \text{ N}$$

**Step 6 — Apply momentum equation in y-direction:**

$$F_{Ry} + 0 - 1776.4 = 188.5 \times (4.243 - 0) = 799.8$$
$$F_{Ry} = 799.8 + 1776.4 = 2576.2 \text{ N}$$

**Step 7 — Force on the bend (sign flip):**

$$F_{bend,\,x} = +12{,}786.5 \text{ N}, \quad F_{bend,\,y} = -2576.2 \text{ N}$$

**Step 8 — Magnitude:**

$$F_{bend} = \sqrt{(12{,}786.5)^2 + (2576.2)^2} = \sqrt{1.635 \times 10^8 + 6.64 \times 10^6}$$
$$F_{bend} = \sqrt{1.701 \times 10^8} = 13{,}043 \text{ N} \approx 13.04 \text{ kN}$$

**Step 9 — Direction:**

$$\alpha = \tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{2576.2}{12{,}786.5}\right) = \tan^{-1}(0.2015) = 11.40°$$

> **Final Answer:** The water exerts a force of **13.04 kN** on the reducing bend, directed at **11.40°** below the +x axis. The anchor block of the bend must be designed to resist this force.

---

### 5.3 KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning

> [!WARNING]
> **Common Mistakes That Cost Marks:**
> 1. **Sign Error on Pressure Thrusts:** The pressure force always acts **inward** on the CV — i.e., opposite to the outward normal $\hat{n}$. Many students add the pressure thrust instead of subtracting it (or vice versa), losing **2–3 marks** consistently.
> 2. **Forgetting Newton's Third Law Sign Flip:** The momentum equation gives the force **on the fluid** from the pipe. The question almost always asks for the force **on the pipe** (or anchor block). Missing this sign flip loses the **final magnitude's sign** — typically **1–2 marks**.
> 3. **Mixing Gauge and Absolute Pressures:** Use **gauge pressure** if the question specifies it; if absolute is given, **subtract atmospheric pressure** first. Mixing them up gives wrong answers.
> 4. **Neglecting the Outlet Pressure Term:** When the outlet is open to atmosphere, $p_2 = 0$ (gauge) — but students sometimes keep it. Always re-read the problem.
> 5. **Wrong Angle Convention:** Define all angles from the **same reference axis** (usually +x). Drawing a small free-body diagram on rough paper before starting the algebra is worth **half a mark** in KTU's structured marking.
> 6. **No Units in Final Answer:** KTU examiners **deduct marks** for missing or wrong units. Always write **N** or **kN**.
> 7. **Forgetting the Direction:** A scalar magnitude alone is incomplete. Always specify the **angle** the force makes with the reference axis.

---

### 5.4 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember

> 📌 **Rapid Revision Checklist — Module 2: Momentum Equations & Pipe Bends**

- ✅ The **Linear Momentum Equation** is Newton's Second Law applied to a control volume: $\sum \vec{F} = \dot{m}(\vec{V}_{out} - \vec{V}_{in})$ for steady, incompressible flow.
- ✅ It is **vector** in nature — always resolve into **x and y** components before solving.
- ✅ The **six standard assumptions** are: steady, incompressible, uniform velocity, hydrostatic pressure, single inlet, single outlet.
- ✅ **Pressure thrust** $pA$ acts **inward** on the control volume at inlet and outlet.
- ✅ The reaction force from the pipe wall on the fluid ($F_R$) is **equal and opposite** to the force the fluid exerts on the pipe (Newton's Third Law).
- ✅ Use **gauge pressure** consistently unless absolute is specified and atmospheric must be subtracted.
- ✅ **Continuity** $A_1 V_1 = A_2 V_2$ is required to find the unknown velocity in reducing/enlarging bends.
- ✅ For a **horizontal bend**, gravity does not enter the x and y momentum equations; it only appears for vertical bends.
- ✅ Final answer should always specify **magnitude (in N or kN) and direction (angle from a chosen axis)**.
- ✅ The formula for force on a 90° horizontal bend (uniform area) is the most frequently asked: $F_x = \rho Q^2 + p_1 A_1$ and $F_y = \rho Q^2 + p_2 A_2$.
- ✅ The momentum equation **does not require** knowledge of frictional losses inside the bend; only the **inlet and outlet** pressures are needed.
- ✅ **Units check:** All terms in the momentum equation are in **Newtons (N)**. Always verify dimensional consistency.
- ✅ **Practical use:** The result is used to design **thrust blocks, anchor supports, and pipe flanges** in water supply, hydropower, and process industries.

---

### 5.5 Quick Reference — Deflection Angles for Common Bends

| Bend Type | Deflection Angle θ | Use Case |
|---|---|---|
| Straight pipe (no bend) | 0° | Continuity only |
| Gentle bend | 15° – 30° | Long-radius elbows in HVAC |
| Standard elbow | 45° | Plumbing and drainage |
| Sharp elbow | 90° | Domestic water supply |
| Return bend | 180° | Heat exchanger U-tubes |
| Y-junction | varies | Branch pipes |

> 💡 **KTU Tip:** Of these, the **90° bend** and **45° reducing bend** appear in **>80%** of past KTU ESE papers from this module. Master these two cases thoroughly.

# SECTION 1: Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

## 1.1 Formal Academic Definition (KTU 2024 Syllabus Terminology)

In the analysis of pipe flow, the **Total Energy Line (TEL)** — also called the **Energy Grade Line (EGL)** — and the **Hydraulic Gradient Line (HGL)** are graphical representations of the energy possessed by a fluid particle as it moves along a streamline.

Applying Bernoulli's equation (with head loss) between any two points in a flow system:

$$
H = z + \frac{p}{\gamma} + \frac{V^2}{2g}
$$

The three terms represent:

| Term | Symbol | Name |
|------|--------|------|
| Elevation above datum | $z$ | Elevation head |
| Pressure energy per unit weight | $\dfrac{p}{\gamma}$ | Pressure head |
| Kinetic energy per unit weight | $\dfrac{V^2}{2g}$ | Velocity head |

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Hydraulic Gradient Line (HGL):** A line joining the **piezometric heads** $\left(z + \dfrac{p}{\gamma}\right)$ at various points along a flow system, plotted above a suitable datum.
>
> **Total Energy Line (TEL):** A line representing the **total head** $\left(z + \dfrac{p}{\gamma} + \dfrac{V^2}{2g}\right)$ at various points along the flow. It is the HGL raised vertically by an amount equal to the local **velocity head** $\dfrac{V^2}{2g}$.

Mathematically, this relationship is:

$$
\text{TEL} = \text{HGL} + \frac{V^2}{2g}
$$

---

## 1.2 Conceptual Analogy — The River-and-Slide Intuition

Imagine a river flowing down a mountain slope (the HGL) and a water-park slide running **parallel** to it but slightly above (the TEL).

- The **river water level (HGL)** shows where fluid would rise in a series of vertical open piezometer tubes connected to the pipe. It captures only the *pressure* and *elevation* energy.
- The **slide (TEL)** is always above the river. The vertical gap between them is the **velocity head** — the extra height a jet of water would shoot upward if a small hole were drilled at that point.

> [!NOTE]
> **Physical Meaning of the Velocity Head Gap:**
> If a Pitot tube is inserted into a flowing pipe, the water rises inside the Pitot by an amount equal to the piezometric head plus the velocity head. This total rise traces the TEL. A simple piezometer tube (open, perpendicular to flow) traces only the HGL.

**Why does this matter in real engineering?**
- If the **HGL falls below the pipe centerline**, the static pressure $p$ is *sub-atmospheric* (negative gauge). This is the principle behind siphons and the danger of cavitation in pumps.
- The **slope of the HGL** gives the *frictional head loss per unit length* — critical for designing long pipelines.

---

## 1.3 Engineering Constants & Standard Metrics

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Key Metric Standards Used in KTU PCCET302:**
> - Acceleration due to gravity: **$g = 9.81 \text{ m/s}^2$**
> - Specific weight of water at standard conditions: **$\gamma_w = 9810 \text{ N/m}^3$**
> - Density of water: **$\rho_w = 1000 \text{ kg/m}^3$**
> - All heads are expressed in **metres of fluid (m)**
> - All pressures in fluid mechanics are typically **gauge pressures** unless specified as absolute.

---

## 1.4 Piezometric Head — The Heart of HGL

The **piezometric head** $h^*$ is the height to which a fluid column rises in an open piezometer tube:

$$
h^* = z + \frac{p}{\gamma}
$$

> [!NOTE]
> **The HGL is simply the locus of piezometric heads along the flow path.** Whenever a pipe has a small vertical tap connected to an open tube, the water level in that tube marks a point on the HGL.

If the HGL lies *above* the pipe, the gauge pressure is **positive**.
If the HGL lies *below* the pipe, the gauge pressure is **negative (vacuum)**, but only physically possible if the absolute pressure remains above the fluid's vapor pressure.
<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
# SECTION 2: Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

## 2.1 Operational Logic — Step-by-Step Theory

### A. The Two Lines and Their Vertical Separation

1. **Compute total head** at any cross-section using the modified Bernoulli equation.
2. **Compute piezometric head** by subtracting the velocity head: $h^* = H - \dfrac{V^2}{2g}$.
3. **Plot both values** above a horizontal datum, then connect consecutive points smoothly.
4. The **vertical distance** between the two lines at any section is exactly $\dfrac{V^2}{2g}$.

### B. Why HGL Rises at a Sudden Enlargement (Counter-Intuitive but True!)

Although **total energy decreases** (TEL drops) at a sudden expansion, the **pressure head increases** dramatically because kinetic energy is converted into pressure energy. Therefore:

- TEL **drops** by an amount equal to the head loss: $h_L = \dfrac{(V_1 - V_2)^2}{2g}$
- HGL **rises** by an amount equal to the pressure recovery: $\Delta h^* = \dfrac{V_2(V_1 - V_2)}{g}$

This is a **classic KTU question** because students often wrongly conclude that HGL must also drop.

### C. Slope of the HGL and TEL

For a pipe of constant diameter $D$ carrying fluid at average velocity $V$ with Darcy friction factor $f$:

$$
\text{Slope of HGL} = \text{Slope of TEL} = S_f = \frac{h_f}{L} = \frac{f V^2}{2gD}
$$

This is called the **friction slope** $S_f$. Since $V$ is constant for a uniform pipe, both lines are **parallel and straight**.

### D. Behavior at Pipe Singularities

| Component | Effect on TEL | Effect on HGL |
|-----------|---------------|---------------|
| Pipe entry from reservoir | Drops by entry loss $0.5 \dfrac{V^2}{2g}$ | Drops by same amount |
| Sudden contraction | Drops by $0.5 \dfrac{V^2}{2g}$ | Drops by same amount |
| **Sudden enlargement** | **Drops by $\dfrac{(V_1-V_2)^2}{2g}$** | **Rises by $\dfrac{V_2(V_1-V_2)}{g}$** |
| Pipe exit to reservoir | Drops by $\dfrac{V^2}{2g}$ (entire velocity head lost) | Drops by $\dfrac{V^2}{2g}$ |
| Pump | Rises by pump head $H_p$ | Rises by same amount |
| Turbine | Drops by turbine head $H_t$ | Drops by same amount |

### E. Why the HGL Can Fall Below the Pipe

If a long pipe is too steep, the elevation head $z$ drops faster than the friction loss accumulates, so $h^* = z + p/\gamma$ may fall below the pipe centerline. As long as $p_{abs} > p_{vapor}$, no cavitation occurs.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Maximum Suction Limit:** A pump can theoretically lift water by 10.33 m at sea level, but practical limits (NPSH) reduce this to 6–7 m. The HGL helps visualize this: a pump's HGL must remain above the impeller.

---

## 2.2 KTU Formula Sheet / Cheat Sheet

| # | Formula | Description | Typical Use |
|---|---------|-------------|-------------|
| 1 | $H = z + \dfrac{p}{\gamma} + \dfrac{V^2}{2g}$ | Total head at a point | Energy analysis |
| 2 | $h^* = z + \dfrac{p}{\gamma}$ | Piezometric head | Traces HGL |
| 3 | $\text{TEL} = \text{HGL} + \dfrac{V^2}{2g}$ | Relationship between lines | Plotting |
| 4 | $h_f = \dfrac{f L V^2}{2gD}$ | Darcy–Weisbach friction loss | Uniform pipe |
| 5 | $S_f = \dfrac{h_f}{L} = \dfrac{f V^2}{2gD}$ | Friction slope (= slope of HGL/TEL for constant D) | Energy line slope |
| 6 | $h_L = \dfrac{(V_1 - V_2)^2}{2g}$ | Sudden enlargement head loss | Pipe fittings |
| 7 | $\Delta h^* = \dfrac{V_2(V_1 - V_2)}{g}$ | Pressure recovery in HGL at enlargement | HGL plotting |
| 8 | $h_{\text{exit}} = \dfrac{V^2}{2g}$ | Exit loss into reservoir | Boundary conditions |
| 9 | $h_{\text{entry}} = 0.5 \dfrac{V^2}{2g}$ | Sharp-edged entry loss | Boundary conditions |
| 10 | $Q = A_1 V_1 = A_2 V_2$ | Continuity equation | Find velocity ratio |

> [!WARNING]
> **Always use $V^2/2g$ separately from $p/\gamma$ and $z$ in Bernoulli's equation.** The most common error in KTU papers is forgetting to convert $p$ to head using $p/\gamma$ before adding $V^2/2g$.

---

## 2.3 Real-World Engineering Utility

1. **Water supply mains:** Engineers plot HGL to ensure pressure at consumer end-points stays above minimum required (typically 7–15 m head).
2. **Pump station design:** HGL reveals whether a pump has adequate NPSH (Net Positive Suction Head) to avoid cavitation.
3. **Sewer and storm drains:** HGL is drawn through manholes to ensure gravity flow (HGL must remain above the crown of pipe for non-pressurized flow).
4. **Hydroelectric penstocks:** TEL shows total available energy for power generation: $P = \gamma Q H_{TEL}$.
5. **Cooling water circuits in thermal power plants:** HGL/TEL diagrams help balance multiple pumps and condensers.

# SECTION 3: Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

## 3.1 Derivation: Head Loss Due to Sudden Enlargement (Borda–Carnot Equation)

**Setup:** A pipe of cross-sectional area $A_1$ carrying fluid at velocity $V_1$ suddenly enlarges to area $A_2$, where the new velocity is $V_2$. The flow is horizontal (no elevation change) and steady. Pressure at section 1 is $p_1$ and at section 2 is $p_2$.

We will combine the **continuity equation**, **momentum equation**, and **energy equation**.

### Step 1 — Apply the Continuity Equation

$$
A_1 V_1 = A_2 V_2 = Q
$$

The discharge is conserved. We can write the velocity ratio:

$$
\frac{A_1}{A_2} = \frac{V_2}{V_1}
$$

### Step 2 — Apply the Momentum Equation (Control Volume Between 1 and 2)

The net pressure force on the fluid in the control volume equals the rate of change of momentum. Note that the pressure force at section 2 acts on the full enlarged area $A_2$ (the annulus is "shaded" by the area change).

$$
\sum F_x = \dot{m}(V_2 - V_1)
$$

$$
p_1 A_2 - p_2 A_2 = \rho A_2 V_2 (V_2 - V_1)
$$

> **Note:** The control volume's right face has area $A_2$ (not $A_1$), so both pressure terms use $A_2$. The mass flow rate at the exit is $\dot{m} = \rho A_2 V_2$.

Dividing through by $\gamma A_2$ (where $\gamma = \rho g$):

$$
\frac{p_1 - p_2}{\gamma} = \frac{V_2 (V_2 - V_1)}{g}
$$

### Step 3 — Apply the Energy Equation (Bernoulli) Between 1 and 2

For horizontal flow with no pump/turbine:

$$
\frac{p_1}{\gamma} + \frac{V_1^2}{2g} = \frac{p_2}{\gamma} + \frac{V_2^2}{2g} + h_L
$$

Rearranging for the head loss:

$$
h_L = \frac{p_1 - p_2}{\gamma} + \frac{V_1^2 - V_2^2}{2g}
$$

### Step 4 — Substitute the Pressure Difference from Step 2

$$
h_L = \frac{V_2 (V_2 - V_1)}{g} + \frac{V_1^2 - V_2^2}{2g}
$$

To combine these terms, bring to a common denominator of $2g$:

$$
h_L = \frac{2 V_2 (V_2 - V_1) + (V_1^2 - V_2^2)}{2g}
$$

Expand the numerator:

$$
2 V_2 (V_2 - V_1) = 2 V_2^2 - 2 V_1 V_2
$$

$$
V_1^2 - V_2^2 = (V_1 - V_2)(V_1 + V_2)
$$

So the total numerator becomes:

$$
2 V_2^2 - 2 V_1 V_2 + V_1^2 - V_2^2 = V_1^2 - 2 V_1 V_2 + V_2^2 = (V_1 - V_2)^2
$$

### Step 5 — Final Result (Borda–Carnot Equation)

$$
\boxed{\, h_L = \frac{(V_1 - V_2)^2}{2g} \,}
$$

> [!NOTE]
> **This is one of the most frequently tested derivations in KTU PCCET302.** Examiners expect you to state the three governing equations (continuity, momentum, energy), show all algebraic manipulation, and arrive at the boxed result.

---

## 3.2 Derivation: Rise in HGL at Sudden Enlargement

The change in piezometric head across the enlargement is the change in pressure head (since $z$ is constant for a horizontal pipe):

$$
\Delta h^* = h^*_2 - h^*_1 = \frac{p_2 - p_1}{\gamma}
$$

From Step 2 above:

$$
\frac{p_1 - p_2}{\gamma} = \frac{V_2 (V_2 - V_1)}{g}
$$

Therefore:

$$
\frac{p_2 - p_1}{\gamma} = -\frac{V_2 (V_2 - V_1)}{g} = \frac{V_2 (V_1 - V_2)}{g}
$$

$$
\boxed{\, \Delta h^* = \frac{V_2 (V_1 - V_2)}{g} \,}
$$

> **Verification (Sanity Check):** If $V_1 > V_2$, then $V_1 - V_2 > 0$, so $\Delta h^* > 0$ — the HGL rises. ✓
> If $V_1 = V_2$ (no enlargement), $\Delta h^* = 0$ — HGL is continuous. ✓
> If $V_1 < V_2$ (a contraction, which physically requires a separate analysis), the formula would give a negative HGL change — but the Borda–Carnot formula $h_L$ for contraction is different.

---

## 3.3 Verification: HGL and TEL Changes Must Be Consistent

We have two derived quantities:

- Drop in TEL = $h_L = \dfrac{(V_1 - V_2)^2}{2g}$
- Rise in HGL = $\dfrac{V_2 (V_1 - V_2)}{g}$

The change in velocity head across the enlargement is:

$$
\Delta\left(\frac{V^2}{2g}\right) = \frac{V_2^2 - V_1^2}{2g} = -\frac{V_1^2 - V_2^2}{2g}
$$

Energy conservation requires:

$$
\text{Drop in TEL} = \text{Drop in HGL} - \Delta\left(\frac{V^2}{2g}\right)
$$

Let us check:

$$
h_L = -\Delta h^* - \frac{V_2^2 - V_1^2}{2g}
$$

$$
\frac{(V_1 - V_2)^2}{2g} = -\frac{V_2 (V_1 - V_2)}{g} - \frac{V_2^2 - V_1^2}{2g}
$$

Convert everything to denominator $2g$:

$$
\frac{(V_1 - V_2)^2}{2g} = \frac{-2 V_2 (V_1 - V_2) - (V_2^2 - V_1^2)}{2g}
$$

The right-hand side becomes:

$$
\frac{-2 V_1 V_2 + 2 V_2^2 - V_2^2 + V_1^2}{2g} = \frac{V_1^2 - 2 V_1 V_2 + V_2^2}{2g} = \frac{(V_1 - V_2)^2}{2g}
$$

This equals the left-hand side. ✓ The derivation is internally consistent.

---

## 3.4 Worked Numerical Example (Foundational)

**Problem:** Water flows through a 15 cm diameter pipe at a velocity of 3 m/s. The pipe suddenly enlarges to 30 cm diameter. Determine:
(a) The head loss due to enlargement
(b) The change in HGL (rise or drop)
(c) The change in TEL (rise or drop)

**Solution:**

### Step 1 — Compute Velocities

The cross-sectional areas are:

$$
A_1 = \frac{\pi}{4}(0.15)^2 = 0.01767 \text{ m}^2
$$

$$
A_2 = \frac{\pi}{4}(0.30)^2 = 0.07069 \text{ m}^2
$$

Using continuity $A_1 V_1 = A_2 V_2$:

$$
V_2 = V_1 \cdot \frac{A_1}{A_2} = 3 \cdot \frac{0.01767}{0.07069} = 3 \cdot 0.25 = 0.75 \text{ m/s}
$$

### Step 2 — Head Loss (Borda–Carnot)

$$
h_L = \frac{(V_1 - V_2)^2}{2g} = \frac{(3 - 0.75)^2}{2 \times 9.81} = \frac{(2.25)^2}{19.62} = \frac{5.0625}{19.62}
$$

$$
\boxed{\, h_L = 0.258 \text{ m} \,}
$$

### Step 3 — Change in HGL

$$
\Delta h^* = \frac{V_2 (V_1 - V_2)}{g} = \frac{0.75 \times 2.25}{9.81} = \frac{1.6875}{9.81}
$$

$$
\boxed{\, \Delta h^* = 0.172 \text{ m (rise in HGL)} \,}
$$

### Step 4 — Change in TEL

The TEL always drops by $h_L$:

$$
\boxed{\, \Delta \text{TEL} = -0.258 \text{ m (drop in TEL)} \,}
$$

### Step 5 — Consistency Check

Change in velocity head:

$$
\Delta\left(\frac{V^2}{2g}\right) = \frac{V_2^2 - V_1^2}{2g} = \frac{(0.75)^2 - (3)^2}{2 \times 9.81} = \frac{0.5625 - 9}{19.62} = -0.430 \text{ m}
$$

Energy balance: Drop in TEL = Drop in HGL − Δ(V²/2g)
$-0.258 = -(-0.172) - (-0.430)$? Let's rewrite:
Drop in TEL = $-0.258$
Drop in HGL = $-0.172$ (negative because it rose by 0.172)
$\Delta(V^2/2g) = -0.430$

$$
\text{Drop in HGL} - \Delta\left(\frac{V^2}{2g}\right) = (-0.172) - (-0.430) = 0.258 = h_L \quad \checkmark
$$

The energy balance is satisfied. **TEL dropped 0.258 m, HGL rose 0.172 m.**
